title: 'Could cripple US tech for more than a generation': Microsoft President Brad Smith on Trump's green-card curbs - TradingView
content: New Delhi, Oct. 15 -- Microsoft President and Vice Chair Brad Smith has warned that the Trump administration's move to restrict green-card access for skilled foreign workers could weaken the US technology sector and push talent towards other countries, Politico reported. In an interview with Politico's Decoded, Smith said blocking pathways to permanent residency for highly skilled immigrants could cripple the US technology industry for more than a generation. His remarks came less than a week after US Vice President JD Vance announced that the administration would bar Microsoft and seven other companies from seeking green cards for skilled foreign workers. Smith also rejected Vance's allegations that Microsoft had abused the H-1B visa programme to avoid hiring American workers at higher salaries, describing the claims as "completely off base". He said the US should be concerned about sending signals that could encourage talented artificial intelligence and software engineers to pursue opportunities in other countries rather than remain in the US. Smith also argued that Microsoft's green-card applications largely concerned long-serving employees rather than new hires, attributing the situation to a lengthy backlog in processing applications. He said someone had failed to provide Vance with accurate information about the company's figures. Smith denied that Microsoft paid foreign-born employees less than American workers. According to Politico, he said the company follows the same compensation system for all employees, irrespective of their immigration status. He also pointed to Microsoft's domestic hiring, saying the company employed more than 9,000 US-born workers last year. Smith argued that this contribution had been overlooked in the administration's criticism of its use of skilled-worker visas. The Microsoft executive called on the White House to reassess its position in light of what he described as a more accurate account of the company's hiring practices. The Donald Trump-led US administration on October 8 suspended the PERM programme for certain IT companies including Microsoft, TCS, Infosys, Wipro and Cognizant among others. The suspension bars the affected companies from submitting new PERM applications and stops the processing of pending applications, according to reports. The Permanent Labour Certification programme, known as PERM, is a process run by the US Department of Labor that allows companies to sponsor foreign employees for US green cards, which grant permanent residency.Disclaimer Published by HT Digital Content Services with permission from MINT. title: Anthropic Reveals a Major Surprise Ahead of Its IPO - TradingView
content: Microsoft MSFT backed Anthropic is heading toward one of the most closely watched technology IPOs in years with a powerful message for prospective investors: revenue is surging, profitability is improving, and the company believes the economics of AI can scale faster than the costs. At a pre-IPO investor meeting in San Francisco, Anthropic told attendees that third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion, up roughly 45% from $11.6 billion in the second quarter and more than triple the $4.7 billion reported in the first quarter, according to Reuters. The company also told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis in Q3, a potentially important milestone as Wall Street becomes more skeptical of AI companies burning enormous amounts of capital. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a valuation of more than $2 trillion for its eventual public listing. That means the company is asking investors to believe its extraordinary growth can justify an equally extraordinary valuation. Anthropic executives also highlighted how Claude is increasingly being used internally, including in work tied to designing a custom chip. CEO Dario Amodei continued emphasizing AI safety, but notably avoided discussing human extinction at the investor event, despite Anthropic previously warning in its prospectus that advanced AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. The company's financial challenge remains enormous. Anthropic has committed at least $518 billion over a decade to cloud services, computing and infrastructure. Last year, revenue reportedly rose twelvefold to nearly $4.6 billion, while operating losses exceeded $8 billion. I think the most striking number is the sequential growth. Revenue moving from $4.7 billion in Q1 to $16.8 billion in Q3 implies an increase of roughly 257% in just two quarters. That kind of growth helps explain why Anthropic believes a $2 trillion-plus valuation is achievable. But the IPO debate will likely come down to one question: can revenue compound faster than infrastructure spending? Adjusted profitability in Q3 is encouraging, but investors will need to determine how durable that profit is once massive cloud and computing commitments are fully reflected. The key metrics to watch are revenue growth, gross margins, adjusted operating income, compute costs, customer concentration and the pace of infrastructure spending. If Anthropic can sustain anything close to its current growth while proving that margins expand with scale, its IPO could become a defining test for the entire AI trade. title: Morgan Stanley finds a new twist in Microsoft's AI story - Yahoo Finance Australia
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results Everyone has been watching the wrong race. While the AI world obsesses over which lab builds the best model, a fresh CIO survey from Morgan Stanley points to a quieter fight playing out beneath the surface, one Microsoft may already be winning. In a note shared with TheStreet on Oct. 12, Morgan Stanley published findings from its third-quarter 2026 AlphaWise CIO survey. The bank maintained its Overweight rating and $600 price target on Microsoft, against a closing price of $541.15 that day. But the more telling data was not about the stock. It was about where enterprise IT chiefs think AI money is actually heading. Also read: Wall Street doubles down on Microsoft stock for investors One of the more interesting questions Morgan Stanley threw into this survey was about AI orchestration. Not which model do you use, but who sits above the models, directing traffic, managing data permissions, keeping an eye on costs. Microsoft pulled 20% of responses on that one. LLM providers collectively were right behind at 17%. Google got 5%, Amazon 4%. That finding runs counter to the popular narrative. The assumption has been that whoever wins the model race wins the enterprise AI race. But a growing number of companies are spreading workloads across multiple models rather than committing to one. The moment a business is running different models for different tasks, it needs something above the models to keep things organized. That is the orchestration layer, and right now Microsoft is where most CIOs say they'd go for it. Microsoft's setup for this is Azure at the infrastructure level, Fabric for enterprise data, Foundry to select and route AI tasks, and Copilot to surface the results inside everyday applications. A company could run a competitor's model through that stack and Microsoft still collects on the infrastructure, the data layer, and the software. Three revenue opportunities from one AI workflow. Thirty percent of CIOs named Microsoft as the vendor most likely to capture the biggest share of generative AI spending in 2026, up from 27% the prior quarter, according to the survey. LLM providers came in at 16%, Google at 8%, Amazon at 7%. Pull back to a three-year horizon and things get messier. Microsoft is at 28%, which was 30% just last quarter. LLM providers climbed from 17% to 21% in that same window. The vendor consolidation story that once looked inevitable hasn't materialized. Companies are running multiple models, and the labs behind those models are now showing up in procurement conversations they weren't part of a year ago. You could read that as bad news for Microsoft. Morgan Stanley doesn't see it that way. Juggling several models creates its own headaches, and someone has to build the tooling that keeps everything organized. That is the business Foundry is going after. Here is something that should give AI bulls pause. Forty-two percent of CIOs told Morgan Stanley they cannot yet measure the returns on their AI token spending. Another 28% say returns are running below what they spend. Only 13% are ahead. Businesses are not waiting around on this. Forty-three percent already have token spend controls in place. Another 31% said they're putting them in before the end of 2027. Add those up and you're looking at most of the enterprise market actively trying to get a grip on what AI is actually costing them. The implication for Microsoft is straightforward. A tool that helps a company route cheaper models for simpler tasks and save the expensive ones for work that actually needs them has a pretty clear value proposition when IT chiefs are being asked to justify every dollar. That is Foundry's pitch, and the survey data suggests the appetite for it is growing. On the cloud side, 79% of surveyed CIOs said their organizations use Azure, ahead of AWS at 66% and Google Cloud at 43%. That maps closely to broader market data showing Azure holding the second largest share of global cloud infrastructure spend behind AWS. Microsoft's net score for expected IT budget share gains in 2026 came in at plus 43%, compared with plus 26% for Amazon and plus 4% for Google. Over the next three years, that gap stays wide: Microsoft at plus 35%, Amazon at plus 11%. Microsoft's $665 target hinges on a new AI advantage Meta and Microsoft just sent employees a memo about Anthropic The caveat is the growth rate. CIOs who use Azure expect spending to grow 15% in 2026, down from 21% in last year's survey for 2025. AWS is right alongside at 15%, with Google Cloud at 12%. Microsoft is still the biggest cloud by usage, but the growth advantage it once had over Amazon is largely gone. The longer runway is in AI workloads themselves. CIOs in the survey put AI and machine learning at 3.8% of their cloud spending today. In three years, they expect that to hit 9.9%. If even half of that growth flows through Azure, the demand picture looks pretty different from what current growth rates suggest. Getting there is another question. CIO surveys are a snapshot of intentions. They are not contracts. A respondent who says Microsoft will get the biggest share of their AI budget in 2026 could face a CFO in January with a very different view. The orchestration preference data is especially early, given that Foundry is still a relatively new product. Morgan Stanley has a $600 price target on Microsoft, but the range around it tells the real story. Their bull case goes to $795. Their bear case drops to $250. A $545 gap between best and worst is a pretty honest admission of how much nobody actually knows. Survey data shows where CIOs say they want to spend. Whether that translates into the numbers Microsoft needs to justify its valuation is a different conversation entirely. What this survey really captures is a change in the question enterprises are asking. It used to be: Which AI model should we use? Now it's: Who keeps all our models working together? That fight doesn't get nearly the attention the model race does, but it might end up mattering more. And right now, when CIOs try to answer it, Microsoft is the name that comes up first. title: Microsoft's Q1 results might produce larger-than-normal beat due to Azure growth: analysts - TradingView
content: Microsoft's MSFT first-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings results appear ripe to produce a larger-than-normal beat due in part to strong growth in its Azure cloud unit, prompting multiple financial firms to increase their price targets on the stock. Shares edged up nearly 1% during Thursday market action. Microsoft shares have surged nearly 40% since releasing its third-quarter results in late July. "We model Azure at 45% CC growth (vs. +44-45% guide, +42% last quarter) and believe the upside should top the outsized ~3% beat last quarter and hit 50%+ levels," said TD Cowen analyst Derrick Wood in an investor note. "3P data we track showed meaningful growth acceleration in new bookings in C3Q for the Big 4 (+125% Y/Y vs. +90% in C2Q), painting a strong backdrop for compute demand. More importantly, we estimate OpenAI OPENAI moving from ~$1b in incremental revs/qtr in 1HCY26 to ~$4-5b/qtr in 2HCY26, which we see as the key source of a larger beat & raise considering MSFT's rev share & inference serving position." TD Cowen retained its Buy rating and increased its target to $625 from $540 ahead of earnings. Meanwhile, UBS also increased its target to $675 from $525 and maintained its Buy rating. "The tricky part of the Microsoft setup is that post the 39% move in the stock since the 4Q/Jun print, Microsoft shares are now a consensus long, rooted in optimism about the Azure and M365 segment upside, confidence in the CFO's margin/EPS control, as well as a belief that the upcoming meetings with Microsoft leadership at the mid-Nov Ignite conference could further improve sentiment," said UBS analyst Karl Keirstead in a note. "But in our view, the 23x CY27 non-GAAP EPS multiple remains reasonable; the fundamentals appear to be relatively clean with a path to upside, and Microsoft shares may warrant a premium for the fact that, amidst plenty of change in the AI market, the company is increasingly model-agnostic and chip-agnostic, with a very diversified portfolio." Finally, Jefferies raised its target to $650 from $575 and maintained its Buy rating. "Azure's 44-45% CC guide leaves room for upside as AI demand continues to outstrip supply and pricing remains strong, while M365 Commercial should accelerate from 15% CC to 17% CC as Copilot drives ARPU expansion," said Jefferies analyst Brent Thill in a note. "Despite elevated AI investment, margins remain resilient, while shares at ~26x NTM P/E vs. a 28x 5-year avg support an attractive R/R." Microsoft is slated to release its Q1 results post-market on October 28. A consensus estimate expects revenue of $90.71B and earnings per share of $4.72. title: Microsoft Went 240 Trading Days Without a Record Close. History Says What Usually Happens Next. - The Motley Fool
content: The stock was higher a year later after five of its seven past waits this long. What went wrong in the other two? Microsoft (MSFT +1.08%) finished Tuesday, Oct. 13, at $543.45, its first record close since Oct. 28, 2025, when shares ended the day at $542.07. All told, 240 trading days passed between the two records. The stock didn't drift sideways in between. It dropped to $352.83 by June 25, around 35% under the last record, before rising about 54% to get back. Microsoft has gone at least 150 trading days without a record close seven other times since it went public in 1986. For five of them, the stock was up a year after the wait ended. For the other two, it was down -- and the two misses have something in common with the wait that just ended. The numbers here use split-adjusted closing prices from March 1986 through Oct. 13. "A year later" means the price on the same date a year after the new record (or the trading day before, if the market was closed), leaving out dividends. The first wait started just two weeks before the stock market crash in October 1987, when the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +1.08%) dropped 22.6% in a day. Microsoft lost around half its value by late October and didn't close at a new record until Oct. 5, 1989, 507 trading days later. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,876,672 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. The 1990s saw three more waits. Each lasted 193 to 241 trading days, with a fall of 24% to 26% along the way. The waits that ended in May 1994 and April 1996 were followed by gains of around 67% and 96% in the next year. But the one that ended in October 1992 was followed by a 9% drop. Then came the long one. The company's record close on Dec. 27, 1999, stood until Oct. 21, 2016, nearly 17 years later. At the March 2009 low, shares traded around 75% under the 1999 record. A year after the 2016 record, they were up about 32%. (With prices that also adjust for dividends, that wait ended in 2014 instead.) The last two waits split. The period from November 2021 to June 2023 saw a 38% fall, and the stock rose around 27% over the next year. The wait from July 2024 to June 2025 had a 24% drop, and shares were about 11% lower a year after it ended. In both misses, the stock kept rising for a few more months after the new record. Then it peaked, and another long wait began. After the October 1992 record, Microsoft rose around 10% further to a record close on June 1, 1993. That close started the 241-trading-day wait that ran till May 1994, and the drop during it dragged the one-year return below zero. The June 2025 record played out almost the same way. Shares gained around 16% more to the Oct. 28, 2025 high, which began the wait that just ended. By June 5, 2026, the stock was around 11% under the June 2025 record. In other words, both misses came from a second long wait starting within months of the first one ending. Notably, the only other time a long wait began within a year of the last one ending was 1993. And when that wait finally ended in May 1994, shares climbed around 67% in the next year. Of course, seven cases are a small sample, and one match might easily be a fluke. I'd put more weight on what the company did while the stock stood still. At the Oct. 28, 2025 record, Microsoft's price-to-earnings ratio was around 40, based on earnings of $13.64 a share in fiscal 2025 (Microsoft's fiscal years end June 30). At Tuesday's record close, it cost around 30 times earnings. That's because earnings per share gained 32% to $17.95 for fiscal 2026. Even leaving out the effect of Microsoft's investment in OpenAI, the non-GAAP (adjusted) number rose 22%. Put another way, each dollar put in the stock at Tuesday's close bought almost a third more earnings than it did at the last record. Microsoft's fiscal 2027 first-quarter report, due Wednesday, Oct. 28, might show if the growth is holding up. All told, five of seven is a decent record. But I wouldn't count on a pattern so thin. What I find more convincing is that Microsoft arguably grew into its valuation while the stock went nowhere. And with adjusted earnings up 22% last fiscal year, paying around 30 times earnings for the stock today seems reasonable to me. Microsoft Corp.(MSFT) announced Friday the launch of a specialized artificial intelligence system designed to execute rapid automated decisions, marking a strategic pivot toward lower-cost, highly targeted AI tools for enterprise workflows. The new software, titled Microsoft-Decision-1, is engineered to handle tasks such as sorting incoming queries, routing system requests, verifying data, and managing autonomous agents. Unlike conventional large language models built around conversational text, decision models are designed to evaluate defined options and output direct, structured metrics that software programs can consume without human intervention. Achint Srivastava, Vice President of Software Engineering at Microsoft's Office of the CTO, said in a statement that decision-scoring systems represent an emerging category intended to address latency bottlenecks in software automation. MSFT stock gained about 2.3% on Friday and ended the week 3.4% higher. A key challenge in multi-step AI operations is accumulated delay. When multiple automated decisions execute sequentially, slight lags at each step can slow down entire applications. To tackle this, Microsoft engineers post-trained a 9-billion-parameter base model (Qwen3.5-9B). In benchmark testing spanning nearly 150,000 blind evaluations, the system recorded the highest accuracy among evaluated models while operating at roughly 35 times the speed of flagship text models such as ChatGPT’s GPT-6 Sol. The model also demonstrated stability against prompt manipulation. Internal evaluations showed the system changed its decision output in only 1.3% of cases when requests were paraphrased or when option orders were re-sorted. Microsoft reported that several internal teams have already deployed the model to streamline operations. For instance, Xbox Research used the tool to categorize more than 10,000 player reviews into structured categories, achieving a 14x speed increase over previous setups. The Microsoft Copilot team used the system for quality assurance checks on interactive agent responses, operating up to 100 times faster than prior configurations. Microsoft-Decision-1 is accessible to developers through Microsoft Foundry, with plans to expand availability to OpenRouter. title: Microsoft Just Unveiled a Brand-New AI Chip. Could It Be the "Nvidia Killer" Everyone's Been Looking For? - The Motley Fool
content: On Monday, Microsoft (MSFT +1.08%) unveiled its latest AI chip architecture, the Maia 300. And the company went out of its way to point out the ways in which the Maia 300 was superior to graphics processing units (GPUs). "This is our biggest bet yet on our own silicon," said CEO Satya Nadella. This was seen as a shot across the bow to the world's premier GPU maker, Nvidia (NVDA -1.84%). So is the Maia 300 the "Nvidia killer" that everyone has been anticipating for years? It might be, but not in the way you might think. Here's what's really going on. The Maia 300 is an upgraded version of the Maia 200, which was released in January. The Maia 200 is currently in production and has already been deployed at Microsoft facilities in Iowa and Arizona, where it's used instead of GPUs and other components from Nvidia, Intel (INTC -2.80%), and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -1.50%). In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,876,672 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Microsoft claims the new, upgraded Maia 300 chip is even more economical and can process 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared to GPUs. A higher token-per-megawatt ratio results in lower AI costs because the biggest expense for an AI data center is electricity. But even if it's cheaper to operate, it's certainly not going to match the power of Nvidia's top-of-the-line systems. Won't that be an issue? Perhaps more than any other company, Microsoft has done very well by coming in second. Its Azure cloud platform is the second-largest, compared to Amazon's Amazon Web Services. Its Surface tablets have never outsold Apple's iPad. Its Xbox has always played second fiddle to the Sony PlayStation. So it shouldn't surprise anyone that Microsoft isn't trying to beat Nvidia at its own game, but to compete on a more favorable playing field: cost. "Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems," Microsoft said in its blog post announcing the Maia 300 system. The company hopes to leverage this to its advantage. Austin Lyons, an analyst for Chipstrat, thinks there's an opportunity here in optimizing different AI processors for different tasks. "The advantage of custom silicon is that Microsoft can optimize for the latency its own workloads actually require," he wrote. "A meeting summary and a coding agent don't need the same response time. Maia targets more throughput at each of those latency points, translates to more useful tokens served per megawatt and lower cost passed for customers." Pat Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy agrees, writing: Microsoft is now moving toward deploying Maia at meaningful production scale. At that scale, custom silicon isn't just about performance. It can become an important margin driver by improving the economics of delivering Microsoft's own AI services. Lyons and Moorhead are echoing commentary from across the industry that suggests the AI race is evolving away from a zero-sum contest to create the fastest, most powerful processors. Hyperscalers and other major players are starting to think about the economics of AI and what customers will be willing to pay in an era where the tech giants start to monetize the new technology. By running lower-difficulty, in-house AI queries on processors that operate more cheaply, Microsoft is taking another step in proactive cost management, which is one of the key reasons investors rewarded the stock earlier this year. So while the Maia 300 isn't an Nvidia killer on its own, it's evidence that the most powerful AI processors -- currently Nvidia's GPUs -- may not be everyone's universal first choice in the future for every application. Routing an AI query to the cheapest infrastructure possible for the difficulty of the problem presented may become the norm. In other words, even if Nvidia continues to produce the best tech in the world for decades to come, its sales volume might suffer regardless. The Maia 300 doesn't even begin production until sometime in 2027. And even then, Nvidia AI infrastructure is almost certain to remain a critical part of Microsoft's AI mix. Just last week, Microsoft started taking preorders for a new Surface Laptop Ultra with a starting price of $2,599. That hefty price tag is thanks to its powerful processor that can run AI models without requiring cloud access. The maker of that incredibly powerful chip? You guessed it: Nvidia. When Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) reports again later this month, one line will draw more attention than the rest: how fast Azure grew. That's a lot of weight for a single business inside a company that also sells Windows, Office, Xbox, and LinkedIn. But Azure has earned the spotlight. Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform. Businesses rent its computing power, storage, and AI tools to run their own apps and models. They pay as they use it, so every new AI workload becomes recurring revenue. In fiscal 2026, Azure's revenue passed $100 billion for the first time, according to CEO Satya Nadella, a milestone that cements Microsoft's standing among the 10 Best Growth Stocks to Buy Now According to Billionaires. The catch is what it costs to keep that engine growing. Whether the stock looks fairly priced comes down to one thing: can Azure's growth keep outrunning the bill? Azure revenue jumped 43% in fiscal Q4 2026, the most recent quarter on the books. That helped lift the Intelligent Cloud segment to $39.3 billion, up 32%. Speed is only half the story, though. The stronger evidence of a moat sits in commercial remaining performance obligation (contracted revenue not yet recognized), which climbed 84% to $678 billion. Enterprise customers don't sign commitments that size with a provider they plan to leave, a massive backlog that cements Microsoft's top ranking on lists like the 10 Best Cloud Computing Stocks to Buy According to Billionaires. Microsoft's other advantage is distribution. Companies already living in Microsoft 365 are an easy sell for AI add-ons, and Microsoft 365 Copilot has topped 30 million paid seats, per Nadella. The broader Microsoft Cloud business brought in $59.3 billion in the quarter, up 27%. Fast growth doesn't mean much if margins buckle under it. In fiscal Q4, revenue and operating income both rose 18%, a sign the cloud boom isn't being bought with thinner profits yet. Earnings need one clarification. GAAP diluted EPS came in at $4.81, but that figure was lifted by net gains tied to Microsoft's OpenAI stake. Non-GAAP EPS of $4.74, up 23%, strips those out, so it's the cleaner read on the operating business. For the full fiscal year, non-GAAP EPS reached $17.28, up 22%. Not everything is humming. More Personal Computing revenue slipped 4%, with Xbox content and services down 10%. That just underlines how much of the story now rests on the cloud. This is the worry that won't go away, and if you own the stock, it's the one worth watching. Capital expenditures hit $35.8 billion in fiscal Q4, against $17.1 billion a year earlier. For the full year, spending reached $115.9 billion, up from $64.6 billion. Those data centers and chips will show up as depreciation for years, whether or not demand holds. If Azure growth cools while the spending keeps climbing, margins are where the pain would show first, a key risk that investors must weigh across the Top 10 AI Stocks That Will Skyrocket. The counterweight is that $678 billion order book. Microsoft isn't building on hope alone; much of the demand it's building for is already under contract. That doesn't erase the risk, but it shrinks it. At a forward P/E of 27.39, as of October 12, investors are paying $27.39 for every $1 of expected earnings. That's a premium to the sector's 22.87, but it's below Microsoft's own 5-year average of 30.50. Growth is what makes the premium defensible. Analysts expect EPS growth of 19.80% in 2028, which is solid for a company already this large. While value investors can find cheaper tech multiples, Microsoft's deep enterprise integration and Copilot expansion firmly position it among the 11 Best Agentic AI Stocks to Buy Right Now. The discount to its own history suggests the market is already pricing in some of the capex risk. That's a reasonable place for the stock to sit heading into the next report. Big-money sentiment has cooled slightly, with 273 hedge funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, down from 282 in the prior one. Short interest is just 0.82% of the float, pointing to relatively limited bearish positioning. The evidence points to a cloud business with growing contracted demand and steady margins, priced below Microsoft's own historical norm. For long-term investors comfortable with heavy spending in exchange for cloud and AI exposure, the setup looks reasonable. What would change that picture is a sharp slowdown from Azure's 43% pace while capital spending keeps rising. If that happens, today's multiple would start to look a lot less forgiving. title: Should Microsoft Stock’s New High Stop You From Buying? - Trefis
content: Most investors apply one rule to a stock like Microsoft (MSFT): buy low and never at the top. Microsoft stock closed near its 52-week high on October 13, 2026, making it the wrong time to buy under that logic. Rather than asking whether the price is too high, market participants should examine the historical performance of Microsoft’s earlier highs. Does that rule hold for Microsoft? Microsoft stock is at a high because the company earns more than it did a year ago. The share price rose 6.4% before dividends over the past year, while net income for the twelve months to June 2026 rose 31.3%. Investors are actually paying less for that profit. The price-to-earnings multiple, which measures what investors pay for each dollar of profit, was 37.3 a year ago and is 30.2 now. That growth is clearest in the cloud business. Revenue from Azure and other cloud services grew 43% in fiscal Q4 2026, the quarter to June. Management noted on that quarter’s call that customer demand continues to exceed available capacity. If you have held Microsoft for years, your biggest question may be taxes, not whether to buy at a high. See how a tax-aware transition works. What Happened After Microsoft Stock’s Earlier Highs? Historical data answers the question of how often Microsoft stock rises in the year following a peak. Since October 2016, counting at most one high every six months, the stock has set 13 earlier 52-week highs with a full year after them. It was higher a year later after 12 of those instances. This table details each of those highs except the earliest, alongside where the stock stood a year later. The 12 most recent of 13 earlier 52-week highs. 52-week highs are counted no more than once every six months. Changes are measured from the close on the day of the high. Split-adjusted closing prices, dividends excluded. The middle result was a gain of 31.1% a year later. A buyer purchasing Microsoft at a high usually experienced a strong following year rather than a trading mistake. The data indicates otherwise for Microsoft. Buying on any trading day over the same years gave a middle gain of 30.2% a year later, just below the result after a high. The rule against buying at the top has not held for the company, making a high about as good a day to buy as any other. Buyers usually face a small dip, but not always. The worst result came after the June 2025 high. A buyer at that time was 12.0% down a year later. That is why the rule is not foolish. Yet the June 2025 high was also the only one after which the stock closed 20% or more below the buying price within the year. The expected dip is generally minimal. After a typical earlier high, Microsoft stock’s lowest close in the following year was 2.4% below the buying price. title: Does The Maia Chip Bet Materially Alter Microsoft’s Operating Margin Outlook? - Trefis
content: Microsoft (MSFT) says its own Maia chips will become the main hardware for running its AI models, reducing its reliance on Nvidia. The news lands while Microsoft is short of capacity: management has told investors for several quarters that demand exceeds supply, and has been spending heavily to add more. So how much of Microsoft’s AI work will move to its own chips, and how soon? MSFT metrics > Market Cap $3.9T · Revenue $332B · Growth 17.8% · Op Margin 47% · P/E 29.7x On Monday, Microsoft said it intends to make Maia its primary architecture for running AI models. It also said it will eventually have multiple gigawatts’ worth of Maia chips. Maia will handle most of the AI work behind Copilot and the company’s other products. The third-generation Maia 300, introduced the same day, rolls out in 2027 and targets lower costs and greater efficiency in running AI workloads. The business closest to the move is Intelligent Cloud, the segment that holds Azure and its AI services. If you have held Microsoft for years, your biggest question may be taxes, not the next quarter. See how a tax-aware transition works. On its July earnings call, management said Microsoft would be among the first cloud providers to deploy AI systems based on AMD Helios and NVIDIA Vera Rubin. Management also said its capital spending had pivoted toward short-lived assets, the CPUs and GPUs that have shorter lead times. Two things are new. First, Microsoft intends its own chip, not an outside supplier’s, to become the primary architecture for running its AI models. Second, the company put a scale on that plan, multiple gigawatts, and named the Maia 300 as the chip behind it. Management’s July forecast, made before the announcement, has capital spending rising in fiscal 2027 and full-year operating margin falling by less than 1 point. Maia is aimed at Intelligent Cloud, Microsoft’s second-largest segment in fiscal 2026, which generated $137.8 billion in revenue (41.5% of total) and grew roughly 30% year-over-year at a 41.4% operating margin. Maia also bears on Microsoft’s capital spending: $115.9 billion over the past twelve months, against $182.9 billion of operating cash flow. Microsoft has put no figure on what Maia will save. On its July earnings call for the fiscal fourth quarter, before the Maia announcement, management described a cloud business short of capacity and chasing efficiency: The Maia plan supports management’s push for efficiency, since the new chip is meant to lower the cost of running AI work. The Maia plan is aimed at Microsoft’s capital spending, which absorbed most of its operating cash flow over the past twelve months. The plan’s effect on the numbers cannot be measured yet. Microsoft has given no savings figure, and the Maia 300 rolls out only in 2027. Capital spending in each quarterly report, alongside the Maia 300 rollout, is the measure to follow. The companies said the approach aims to reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen cloud workload security. The working group plans to define an open specification incorporating a hardware security boundary, key vault and attestation chain directly into servers. Most of Microsoft's revenue and profit still come from software sold per user, and that business is at risk if AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic keep improving their own products. title: Microsoft Just Took Its Biggest Step Toward Independence From Nvidia - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Microsoft just announced a chip that could quietly drain billions from Nvidia's most reliable revenue stream, and the full consequences for both companies will not arrive until 2027. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) closed at $541.15, up 1.14%. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) closed at $226.32, down 1.29%. The stocks moved apart after Microsoft revealed Azure Maia 300, its newest in-house AI chip, and said Maia will become the main engine for running its own AI products. Investors treated the news as a small transfer of value from one company to the other. The money involved is in inference, which is the work of running a trained AI model to answer a user. Training is the work of building the model in the first place, so inference is the bill that repeats forever, while training is the bill you pay to get started. Microsoft is building its own hardware for the repeating, high-volume bill and will keep leasing Nvidia silicon for training. If you own Microsoft, the question is who keeps the savings as Copilot and Office turn AI into everyday work. Scott Guthrie, Microsoft’s executive vice president for cloud and AI, wrote: “We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027,” making Maia “the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services.” Satya Nadella posted on X on October 12, 2026: “Today we are announcing our biggest bet yet on our own silicon.” Large-scale deployment begins in 2027. Reports put possible deployment at more than a million chips next year, but Microsoft has not confirmed that figure. Rani Borkar, who runs Azure’s hardware systems, described the goal as “basically delivering more intelligence for every watt, every dollar, and every byte of memory.” Microsoft says Maia 300 produces 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems. Its 96-chip rack draws about 167 kilowatts, compared with 142 kilowatts for a 72-GPU Nvidia GB300 rack. So each Maia rack uses more power, while Microsoft claims it does more work for each unit of that power. Maia is reserved for Microsoft’s internal use and pays off only by bringing down what it costs Microsoft to serve the Copilot and OpenAI models it already sells, which makes the return smaller than a chip-selling business would offer but much more certain. Microsoft expects capital spending of more than $175 billion this calendar year. At that size, even a small cut in the cost per token means meaningful savings. The program is building on itself, too. Nadella said Maia 200 delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest hardware already in Microsoft’s fleet. Nvidia carries a market value of $5.46 trillion, compared with Microsoft’s $4.02 trillion. Evercore ISI estimates that Maia will account for about 10% of Microsoft’s AI chip spending by early 2027. The bigger risk to Nvidia plays out over years, because inference becomes the larger workload over time and every major cloud company is building chips for it. Nvidia still has training demand that keeps growing, and Microsoft plans to be among the first clouds to roll out Nvidia’s Vera Rubin systems. Every Maia figure comes from Microsoft. Analyst Patrick Moorhead pointed out that “nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet.” Maia’s own plan has slipped before, and an earlier generation’s delay raised questions about later targets. A Microsoft general manager also said the company keeps “a little bit of optionality” because the industry changes fast. The announcement left out training, leasing Maia to customers, and retiring any existing Nvidia capacity. The chips also depend on an outside foundry’s 2-nanometer process, which is in heavy demand. Maia cuts the cost of products Microsoft already sells in huge volume, and that kind of margin gain would accrue to long-term holders, although the 2027 timeline means the savings are still ahead. The stock trades at a trailing P/E of 30. Among the companies affected by this announcement, Microsoft has the clearest upside. The next checkpoint is Microsoft’s earnings call on October 28. If management reports Maia deployment progress or better cloud gross margins, the case holds up. If it says nothing on either, the 2027 promise deserves more doubt. title: Microsoft’s CEO Just Called for a Kill Switch on AI. Here Is What It Means for the Stock. - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Satya Nadella publicly asked for a way to stop his own AI products cold, and the reasoning behind that request has real consequences for whether Microsoft's massive spending bet pays off. Satya Nadella spent a weekend post saying that AI systems need emergency off switches, by which he means authorized humans who can shut a model down in the middle of a task. The idea stands out. He runs Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction), the company with the greatest commercial exposure to frontier AI, and he is publicly asking for a way to stop his own product mid-sentence. Here is the key passage in full: “We can’t treat superintelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers and actions. We must build containment systems whose behavior we can observe, limits that we can test, and actions we can always contain.” For investors, this is a product decision. Microsoft holds about a 27% stake in OpenAI and spent $115.95 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal 2026. Now it wants to sell customers the controls that can stop those systems. The timing matters because over the past year the stock rose only 6.78%, while the S&P 500 gained 19.15%. In engineering terms, an emergency off switch is four ordinary pieces of software, the first of which is a set of breakpoints inside long-running agent tasks, so a person can pause the job between steps. The second is permission scopes that limit which files, systems, and accounts an agent can touch, and the third is logging that records what the agent did and why it did it. The fourth is an identity layer that decides who is allowed to stop the agent. Companies already buy every one of these tools to manage their employees. Microsoft already sells the version built for agents. Agent 365 had nearly 40 million agents registered two months after it launched. The most useful idea in this debate is what you might call the verification tax. If employees spend hours checking what a model produced, the checking eats part of the promised productivity gain. Customers stop renewing software whose output they cannot trust, and renewal rates are how this industry gets valued. Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats. Purview, Microsoft’s compliance tool, tracked more than 15 billion Copilot interactions, up nearly 360% year over year. That audit volume shows customers already want a record of what the AI did. When a system’s behavior can be observed, checking it costs less, and that protects the renewal. Governance, audit trails, and permissions are enterprise software problems. Microsoft already runs the identity and compliance layer where corporate customers manage their people, so selling control over agents extends a business it already has. Nadella has said “every model is substitutable,” and Azure AI Foundry offers more than 11,000 models. If you can swap one model for another, the lasting value sits in the control layer around them. A more cynical read has merit. The incumbent with the largest frontier position gains when safety rules raise the cost of entry for everyone behind it, because only well-funded companies can afford to make powerful models observable, testable, and interruptible. That incentive can exist even if Nadella’s concern about safety is genuine. The market wants to see a return on the spending before it shows up in reported numbers. Fourth-quarter capex was $35.80 billion, up 109.6%, and management expects fiscal 2027 spending to grow again.
